facts.statement: Citipati remains were first collected in the 1990s at the Ukhaa Tolgod locality within the Djadochta Formation.
facts.quote: It is primarily known from the Ukhaa Tolgod locality of the Djadochta Formation, where its remains were first collected during the 1990s.

facts.statement: Citipati lived in Asia during the Late Cretaceous, approximately 75 to 71 million years ago.
facts.quote: Citipati (; meaning "funeral pyre lord") is a genus of oviraptorid dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous of Asia, approximately 75 to 71 million years ago.

facts.statement: Citipati was among the largest oviraptorids, with an estimated length of 2.5 to 2.9 meters and a weight of 75 to 110 kilograms.
facts.quote: Citipati was among the largest oviraptorids; measuring an estimated 2.5 - 2.9 m in length and weighing 75 - 110 kg.

facts.statement: Citipati possessed toothless upper and lower jaws that ended in a horny beak.
facts.quote: Both the upper and lower jaws were toothless and terminated in a horny beak.

facts.statement: Citipati's tail ended in a pygostyle, a fused structure of the final caudal vertebrae that supported large tail feathers.
facts.quote: The tail ended in a pygostyle, a structure formed by the fusion of the final caudal vertebrae and associated with the support of large rectrices.

facts.statement: Citipati had long feathers on its arms and tail, which may have protected eggs and young from the elements.
facts.quote: The arms and tail were covered with long feathers, which may have provided protection for the eggs and young from exposure to the elements.

facts.statement: Citipati may have been omnivorous, as juvenile troodontid remains found in a nest suggest adults might have brought prey to feed their young.
facts.quote: Citipati may have been omnivorous, as the remains of two juvenile troodontid were discovered in a nest, suggesting that they may have been prey brought by an adult Citipati to feed its young.

facts.statement: A small fossilized oviraptorid embryo (specimen IGM 100/971) was discovered in 1993 at the Ukhaa Tolgod locality in the Gobi Desert during a joint expedition by the Mongolian Academy of Sciences and the American Museum of Natural History.
facts.quote: In 1993, a small fossilized oviraptorid embryo, labelled as specimen IGM 100/971, was discovered in a nest at the Ukhaa Tolgod locality of the highly fossiliferous Djadokhta Formation, Gobi Desert, during the Mongolian Academy of Sciences-American Museum of Natural History paleontological project.

facts.statement: In 2001, James M. Clark, Mark A. Norell, and Rinchen Barsbold named Citipati osmolskae based on holotype IGM 100/978 and referred specimens IGM 100/971 and IGM 100/979 to the genus.
facts.quote: In 2001, the paleontologists James M. Clark, Mark A. Norell and Rinchen Barsbold named the new genus and type species Citipati osmolskae based on the now regarded holotype IGM 100/978, and referred specimens IGM 100/971 (embryo) with 100/979 ("Big Mama").

facts.statement: The generic name Citipati is derived from Sanskrit words meaning 'funeral pyre lord,' referencing a figure in Tibetan Buddhism folklore.
facts.quote: The generic name, Citipati, is formed from the Sanskrit words citi (meaning funeral pyre) and pati (meaning lord) in reference to the lord of cemeteries in the Tibetan Buddhism folklore, Citipati, which is often depicted as a humanoid skeleton.

facts.statement: The specific name osmolskae honors the Polish paleontologist Halszka Osmólska for her work on Mongolian theropods.
facts.quote: The specific name, osmolskae, is in honor to the noted Polish paleontologist Halszka Osmólska, whose work dealt extensively with Mongolian theropods.

facts.statement: A larger and more complete specimen (IGM 100/978) was found in 1994 at the Ankylosaur Flats sublocality by the American Museum–Mongolian Academy of Sciences expeditions.
facts.quote: A larger and more complete specimen, catalogued as IGM 100/978, was found in 1994 also from the Ankylosaur Flats sublocality by the American Museum–Mongolian Academy of Sciences field expeditions.

facts.statement: In 1995, a second nesting oviraptorid specimen (IGM 100/1004), nicknamed 'Big Auntie,' was discovered at the Death Row sublocality by the Mongolian Academy of Sciences-American Museum of Natural History expedition.
facts.quote: In 1995, the Mongolian Academy of Sciences-American Museum of Natural History expedition discovered a second nesting oviraptorid specimen from the Ukhaa Tolgod locality, in a region called Camel's Humps, at the Death Row sublocality. This new specimen was labelled as IGM 100/1004 and nicknamed "Big Auntie".

facts.statement: Specimen IGM 100/1004 was not formally referred to Citipati osmolskae until 2018, despite being discovered in 1995.
facts.quote: Despite being discovered in 1995, the specimen IGM 100/1004 remained partially figured and largely undescribed for years until its formal referral to the taxon Citipati osmolskae in 2018 by Norell and team.

facts.statement: The skull anatomy of the holotype was described in 2002, furcula morphology in 2009, and caudal vertebrae (including the pygostyle) in 2014.
facts.quote: The skull anatomy of the specimen was later described by Clark and colleagues in 2002, the furcula morphology in 2009 by Sterling J. Nesbitt with team, and the caudal vertebrae by W. Scott Persons and colleagues in 2014 who noted the presence of a pygostyle.

facts.statement: It is debated whether remains from the nearby Zamyn Khondt locality represent a second species of Citipati.
facts.quote: A second species may be represented by remains from the nearby Zamyn Khondt locality.

facts.statement: Citipati was a large-bodied oviraptorid estimated to be 2.5 to 2.9 meters long and weigh between 75 and 110 kilograms.
facts.quote: Citipati was a large-bodied oviraptorid, with the largest individuals being emu-sized animals; it has been estimated at 2.5 - 2.9 m in length with a weight between 75 - 110 kg

facts.statement: Citipati possessed an unusually long neck and a shortened tail compared to most other theropods.
facts.quote: Like other oviraptorids, Citipati had an unusually long neck and shortened tail compared to most other theropods.

facts.statement: The presence of a pygostyle and brooding posture in Citipati specimens indicates it had large wing and tail feathers and plumage.
facts.quote: The presence of a pygostyle and the brooding pose in specimens of Citipati indicate the presence of large wing and tail feathers, and plumage.

facts.statement: Citipati had an unusually short, highly pneumatized skull ending in a stout, toothless beak.
facts.quote: Its skull was unusually short and highly pneumatized (riddled with air-spaced openings), ending in a stout, toothless beak.

facts.statement: In 2020, Gregory F. Funston and colleagues established the new subfamily Citipatiinae to separate Citipati from Oviraptor.
facts.quote: However, in 2020, Gregory F. Funston and colleagues found Oviraptor to be more basal, so they named a new subfamily Citipatiinae.

facts.statement: A 2022 study estimated Citipati's bite force to be between 349.3 N and 499.0 N.
facts.quote: A 2022 study of the bite force of Citipati and comparisons with other oviraptorosaurs such as Incisivosaurus, Khaan, and Conchoraptor suggests that Citipati had a very strong bite force, scored between 349.3 N and 499.0 N.

facts.statement: Citipati likely fed on tougher vegetation than other herbivorous theropods in its environment.
facts.quote: The moderate jaw gape seen in oviraptorosaurs is indicative of herbivory in the majority of the group, but it is clear they were likely feeding on much tougher vegetation than other herbivorous theropods in their environment

facts.statement: Citipati eggs are the largest known definitive oviraptorid eggs, measuring 18 cm in length.
facts.quote: The eggs of Citipati are the largest known definitive oviraptorid eggs, at 18 cm.

facts.statement: Citipati nesting specimens were found sitting on top of egg clutches with limbs spread symmetrically and front limbs covering the nest perimeter.
facts.quote: The two nesting specimens of Citipati are situated on top of egg clutches, with their limbs spread symmetrically on each side of the nest, front limbs covering the nest perimeter.

facts.statement: Analysis of brooding posture suggests Citipati had long pennaceous feathers and a full feather covering.
facts.quote: Hopp and Orsen indicated that long pennaceous feathers and a feather covering were most likely present in life.

facts.statement: In 2019, Leas Hearn and team suggested a Citipati individual survived a healed ulna injury to lay and incubate its nest.
facts.quote: As the ulna features positive signs of healing, in 2019 Leas Hearn and team suggested that this individual managed to survive an injury that would have interfered with foraging for several weeks in order to lay and incubate its nest.

facts.statement: Researchers debated whether the Zamyn Khondt oviraptorid specimen represents a second species of Citipati.
facts.quote: They considered this oviraptorid to belong to the genus, however, they could neither confirm nor disregard that this specimen represents a second species of Citipati.

facts.statement: It is debated whether juvenile troodontid skulls found near Citipati nests were prey, nest raiders, or evidence of nest parasitism.
facts.quote: It is possible that these tiny troodontids were preyed upon by the Citipati to feed its nest. Alternately, Mark Norell suggested that the juvenile troodonts were raiding the Citipati nest, or even that an adult Byronosaurus had laid eggs in a Citipati nest as an act of nest parasitism.

facts.statement: Citipati lived approximately 71 to 75 million years ago during the Late Cretaceous period.
facts.quote: Citipati is vastly known from the Ukhaa Tolgod locality of the Djadokhta Formation, which is dated around 71 million to 75 million years ago (Late Cretaceous).

facts.statement: Citipati inhabited arid to semiarid environments consisting of large sand dunes and short-lived water bodies.
facts.quote: The settings in which Citipati and associated paleofauna lived are interpreted as large dune fields/sand dunes and several short-lived water bodies with arid to semiarid climates.

facts.statement: The genus Citipati was named by Clark, Norell, and Barsbold in 2001.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Clark, Norell, & Barsbold, 2001

facts.statement: The species C. osmolskae was named by Clark, Norell, and Barsbold in 2001.
facts.quote: species_authority: Clark, Norell, Barsbold, 2001

facts.statement: At least four specimens of Citipati have been found in nesting positions, including the famous specimen known as 'Big Momma'.
facts.quote: De este gran ovirraptórido con cresta se han encontrado por lo menos 4 ejemplares en posición de anidación, entre ellos el más famoso «Big Momma».

facts.statement: The largest Citipati were about the size of emus, reaching nearly 3 meters in length.
facts.quote: Los más grandes citipati eran animales del tamaño de emúes, con cerca de 3 metros de largo

facts.statement: Citipati had an unusually small, highly pneumatized skull ending in a strong toothless beak.
facts.quote: Su cráneo fue extrañamente pequeño y altamente pneumatizado (acribillado con aberturas en la estructura ósea), terminando en un fuerte pico sin dientes.

facts.statement: The most distinctive feature of Citipati was its high crest, which was superficially similar to that of the modern cassowary.
facts.quote: Tal vez la mayor característica distintiva del Citipati fue su alta cresta, superficialmente similar a la del casuario moderno.

facts.statement: Citipati fossils were found specifically in the Djadokhta Formation at Ukhaa Tolgod in the Gobi Desert of Mongolia.
facts.quote: Fue encontrado específicamente en la Formación de Djadochta de Ukhaa Tolgod, en el desierto de Gobi de Mongolia.

facts.statement: Citipati is one of the best-known oviraptorids due to the number of well-preserved skeletons, including several found incubating on nests with eggs.
facts.quote: Es uno de los ovirraptóridos mejor conocidos, gracias al número de esqueletos bien preservados, incluyendo varios especímenes encontrados en posicione de incubar, encima de nidos con huevos.

facts.statement: The famous specimen 'Big Momma' was discovered in 1995, described in 1999, and assigned to the genus Citipati in 2001.
facts.quote: El más famoso fue llamado «Big Momma» ("Gran Mamá" o "Abuela" en inglés) y fue descubierto, mas no nombrado, en 1995; descrito en 1999, y referido al género Citipati en 2001.

facts.statement: The nesting posture of Citipati supports the hypothesis that it and other oviraptorids had feathered forelimbs.
facts.quote: La posición para anidar del Citipati apoya también la hipótesis de que este y otros oviraptóridos tenían miembros anteriores con plumas.

facts.statement: Citipati eggs are the longest of all oviraptorids, measuring 18 cm.
facts.quote: Los huevos de Citipati son los más largos de todos los ovirraptóridos, con 18 cm

facts.statement: It is debated whether the IGN specimen represents a second species of Citipati or a completely distinct genus.
facts.quote: El espécimen IGN presenta una relación más próxima al Citipati, del cual puede representar una segunda especie o, inclusive, un género completamente distinto.

facts.statement: The time range for Citipati is recorded as 83.6 to 72.2 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Campanian to Campanian (83.6 to 72.2 million years ago)
